newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission tries to hammer out energy tax deal.
newsitem.headline: Commission tries to hammer out energy tax deal.

text.p: European Commission cabinet chiefs will meet later on Monday to iron out differences over a proposal to raise minimum taxation on motor and heating fuels and extend it to electricity and natural gas.

The proposal is tentatively on the agenda for the Commission's weekly meeting on Wednesday, but it could be delayed. "Rumours are that it will be postponed," said an official who is close to the cabinet of Internal Market and Taxation Commissioner Mario Monti.

Another official said the debate now focuses on three aspects: how to ensure that the increased rates are 'fiscally neutral'; whether the proposed levels for 1998, 2000 and 2002 would be indicative or compulsory; and taxation of electricity, gas and diesel.
The proposal for a draft directive on energy taxation foresees an EU-wide minimum tax on motor diesel of 310 European currency units per 1,000 litres in 1998, 343 Ecus in 2000 and 393 Ecus in 2002.

The proposed levels have been lowered following criticism from the industry and within the Commission, but they remain controversial. The existing EU minimum rate for diesel is 245 Ecus and the actual rates in the 15-nation range from 252 Ecus in Greece, where it is the lowest, to 414 Ecus in Britain -- the highest rate.
Monti's staff has also proposed that energy-intensive companies -- measured in terms of energy spending compared with turnover -- may be reimbursed the tax.

But those moves have apparently done little to assuage Industry Commissioner Martin Bangemann's concerns about Europe's competitiveness and the prospect that some countries would reimburse the tax and others not. That would add to tax competition in the Union, one of the problems the current proposal aims to combat.

In a move that highlights the issue's sensitivity, the two British commissioners are reported to be worried that the media will interpret the proposal as a tax increase, which could affect the country's upcoming general elections.

The Spanish commissioners have brought up the recent painful strike of their lorry drivers, while the French representatives have defended their country's powerful nuclear electricity lobby, a Commission official said.
While EU commissioners are supposed to represent the entire EU, not just their own countries, such domestic concerns often influence their positions.

The draft proposes that production of electricity be taxed one Ecu per megawatt/hour in 1998, increasing to 2.0 Ecus in 2000 and 3.0 Ecus in 2002. But aides to Economic Affairs Commissioner Yves Thibault de Silguy have argued for a tax that does not penalise nuclear power, which is non-polluting.

The Commission's proposal arises directly from a demand by EU leaders to build on existing EU legislation on energy excise duties to compensate for the failure of the EU to agree a tax on carbon dioxide emissions from burning fossil fuels.
The move would supplement an agreement by EU environment ministers on Monday to cut the bloc's emissions of greenhouse gases by 15 percent of 1990 levels by 2010.
To smooth approval of the text, the Commission may decide to condition the third round of tax increases in 2002 to a report on the impact of the first two rounds, one source said.
It is also expected to insist that EU states use any additional revenue from energy taxation to lower labour costs, so that it would not increase a country's overall tax burden.
EU finance ministers must agree the energy tax proposals uanimously.
